title: Slipping out
hook: Muslims leave Mecca quietly, in small groups, leaving homes and property

segments.voice: Yesterday: the second pledge at Aqaba. Your line was: protect him as your own.

A door closes in Mecca before dawn, and the family behind it isn't coming back. With the pledge made, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells his followers they can go: God has given them brothers in Yathrib and a home to go to. So they go. Not all together. In ones and twos and families, quietly, so Quraysh won't stop them. Houses are left standing behind them. Today: slipping out.
screen: `A DOOR CLOSES BEFORE DAWN.` → `IN ONES AND TWOS.` → `HOUSES LEFT STANDING.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq keeps some of these departures in close-up. One is Umm Salama's. She sets out with her husband, Abu Salama, and their little son. Her own clan stops them and takes her back: you can go, they tell him, but not with our daughter. Then his clan arrives, furious, and takes the child: if you've kept her, we keep our boy. In a single stop on the road, a family is pulled into three pieces. Abu Salama goes on to Yathrib alone. Umm Salama, in her own telling, goes out every morning to the place where it happened and weeps until evening, for a long time, until a relative takes pity and persuades the clans to let her go. She gets her son back and sets out alone, on a camel, with the boy in her lap. Another is Suhayb, called the Roman, who had come to Mecca with nothing and done well in trade. As he leaves, the story goes, men of Quraysh block him: you came here poor and grew rich among us, and now you'll leave with it all? He asks: if I give you my wealth, will you let me pass? They say yes, and he hands it over. When the Prophet hears, tradition says he answered: Suhayb has made a profitable trade. That's what slipping out looked like. Not a march. A long series of private losses: a house, savings, a morning by the road. The Qur'an speaks of those who emigrated and were driven from their homes and their wealth. These are some of their faces.
screen: `A FAMILY PULLED INTO THREE.` · `WEEPING EACH MORNING.` · `SUHAYB HANDS OVER HIS WEALTH.` · `A PROFITABLE TRADE.` · then, large: `THEY LEFT EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're carrying that you've known for a while you need to put down: a grudge, a habit, a conversation you replay at night. Picture setting it down by the road, the way those families left their doors, not angrily, just leaving, and notice how much lighter you might travel without it. If you pray, you can ask God to help you not turn back for it.
Slipping out. The believers left Mecca quietly in small groups, leaving houses, wealth, and sometimes family behind on the road to Yathrib. Today's word.
Your line: they left everything. Every departure had its own private cost. Day seven hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims call those who left Mecca for Medina the Muhajirun, the emigrants, and retell stories like Umm Salama's and Suhayb's to honor what the hijra cost them.

original.note: Arabic: an emigrant, one who leaves home for the sake of God.

trapdoor: what you thought: the believers moved to another town.
what it means: each one left something real behind: a house, savings, for a time even a child.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq's accounts of Umm Salama and Suhayb; the Qur'an speaks of emigrants driven from their homes and property (59:8).

chat.says: When the early Muslims moved to Medina, was it one big organized move?
options: No. They slipped out quietly in ones and twos, each leaving something behind.
Yes. They all left together in one caravan, with an armed guard.
No. Only the men went north; the families stayed in Mecca for good.
chat.meaning: They went quietly, in ones and twos and families. Umm Salama's family was torn apart for a time; Suhayb gave up his wealth to pass.

Umm Salama.meaning: an emigrant whose family was pulled apart on the road

Abu Salama.meaning: Umm Salama's husband, who went on to Yathrib alone

Suhayb.meaning: called the Roman; gave up his wealth to leave

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the Prophet permits the emigration; Umm Salama's account of her separation; Suhayb gives up his wealth; 'Suhayb has made a profitable trade')
Qur'an 59:8 (emigrants driven from their homes and their belongings)

notes: Umm Salama's account: she says she went out every morning for about a year; the script says 'for a long time' to stay within the claims rule. Confirm.
Suhayb's story and the Prophet's words are paraphrased from the sirah as recalled; some commentators link Qur'an 2:207 to Suhayb (not used here). Confirm.
